text: Exodus 12 moves from "a lamb" to "the lamb" to "your lamb." That's the journey of knowing Jesus.
explanation:
God told Israel, "Every man shall take for himself a lamb… a lamb for a household." Then, "if the household is too small for the lamb…" And finally, "Your lamb shall be without blemish."

At first Jesus is one lamb among many, one teacher among others. Then you realise He is the Lamb, the only one. Finally He becomes your Lamb, personally. And it was always "a lamb for a household": believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your house.

text: The Passover lamb was chosen on the tenth of Nisan and inspected until the fourteenth. Jesus rode into Jerusalem on the tenth and was questioned for days.
explanation:
Each family took their lamb into the house on the tenth day of the month and kept it until the fourteenth, watching for any blemish. On Palm Sunday, Jesus entered Jerusalem. For the next days, priests, Pharisees and Sadducees tested Him in the temple with question after question. Finally He asked them, "What do you think about the Christ?" and "no one dared question Him anymore."

The Lamb of God was examined in public and found without blemish. Then, on Passover, He was slain. "He did no sin… He knew no sin… in Him is no sin." Your Lamb is perfect, and so is your standing through Him.

text: Darkness covered Egypt for three days, "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings."
explanation:
The ninth plague was a darkness so thick it could be felt. No one in Egypt could see anyone else or move from where they were. Yet in every Israelite home there was light, and it wasn't from lamps, because those were available to the Egyptians too.

The world may grow darker in its confusion about right and wrong, about authority, even about who we are. But "the Lord will arise over you, and His glory will be seen upon you." Pray for supernatural light in your home, in your children's hearts and in your family's values.

text: Jesus wept as the crowds praised Him. Don't let flattery puff you up or criticism make you bitter.
explanation:
As Jesus rode down the Mount of Olives, the crowds were shouting, "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!" Most people would have been carried away by the moment. Jesus looked at Jerusalem and wept: not quiet tears, but deep sobbing over the people who didn't recognise their day of visitation.

He was moved by love, not applause. A mark of maturity is being independent of both flattery and censure. Let neither praise nor criticism set your direction; draw your worth from the Lord.

text: At Passover, one of three matzahs, the middle one, is broken, wrapped in cloth, hidden, then found. The finder receives a gift.
explanation:
In the modern Passover seder, three pieces of unleavened bread sit in a cloth pouch. The middle one is taken out and broken; half of it, called the afikoman (a Greek word, not Hebrew), is wrapped in linen and hidden. Later the children search for it, and whoever finds it gets a reward. It's the last thing eaten at the meal.

The tradition isn't in Exodus. But see the picture: Father, Son and Spirit; the Son broken, wrapped in linen by Joseph and Nicodemus, hidden in a tomb, then brought back. For many, the Messiah is still hidden. Those who find Him receive the gift of eternal life.

text: "He brought them out with silver and gold, and there was none feeble among His tribes."
explanation:
God had told Abraham centuries earlier: "Afterward they shall come out with great possessions." On Passover night, Israel left Egypt with the silver and gold the Egyptians freely gave them, generations of unpaid wages returned in a single night. And not one of them was weak or sick.

The night of the Passover lamb brought both health and provision. That's not greed; it's God's faithfulness. Don't try to get back what was taken from you by cheating or manipulation. "The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous." Be patient, and trust God's favour.

text: "This month shall be your beginning of months." God can give you a new start in the middle of your year.
explanation:
Israel's civil year began in the autumn. But at the Passover, God reset their calendar: "This month shall be your beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year to you." Redemption became their new starting point.

You may have made foolish decisions, or things you deeply regret. When the Lamb comes into your story, He resets the clock. "Do not remember the former things… Behold, I will do a new thing." Your new beginning isn't on a calendar date; it's at the cross.
